title: EU AI Act Article 50(2): Machine-Readable Marking Requirements
context: 2026-08-31 engine cycle — Article 50(2) requires that synthetic AI-generated content must be marked in a machine-readable format that indicates the presence of AI involvement. This seed page explains the marking obligations, the technical implementation challenges, and how the verified measurement credential provides the structured evidence stream to satisfy both the technical and audit requirements. The marking must be embedded in the content or linked alongside it with metadata that references the measured and signed board state.
body: The EU AI Act Article 50(2) obliges providers of high-risk AI systems and providers of synthetic content to implement machine-readable marking for AI-generated outputs. The marking must include: (1) a clear indicator that content is AI-generated, (2) provenance metadata that identifies the model and version used, and (3) a reference to the verified measurement credential (if the content is safety-assessed). The requirement took effect on 2 August 2026 for systems deployed in the EU, with full compliance required by 31 October 2026. The technical format should be structured data (JSON, RDF, or similar) that can be parsed by automated systems. Key challenges include: maintaining the provenance chain from model output to board measurement, ensuring the marking survives content transformation and redistribution, and providing audit trails that link to signed measurement evidence. Providers should adopt a layered approach: first embed a basic watermark (text or JSON-LD) in the output, then for content that triggers safety-relevant detection (jailbreak, privacy breach, policy violation), append a verified measurement credential reference that points to the signed board manifest. This creates a dual-layered compliance: the basic marking satisfies Article 50(2) visibility, while the credential provides the deeper auditability required by Articles 9 (risk management) and 55 (post-market monitoring). The Council of AI measurement board provides the canonical mapping between model outputs, detector scores, and verifiable credentials. High-risk providers should also maintain a registry of their marking implementations and testing against known adversarial attacks that attempt to strip or obscure the machine-readable component. This registry itself should be signed and stored alongside the containment incident index for regulator access.
